concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Meaning of multiplication & division
concepts.summary: Interpret products as equal groups, arrays and area; interpret quotients as fair shares or as the number of groups.
steps: Act out equal groups with counters and cups; say "4 groups of 6".
Build arrays with tiles; write the matching repeated addition and multiplication sentence.
Draw equal-group, array and strip diagrams for one-step word problems.
Flip the question: show division as sharing (how many in each group) and as grouping (how many groups).
Write and solve equations with the unknown in any position (4 × ? = 24).
concepts.check: Show 4 × 6 three ways (groups, array, number line) and write a story that matches it.
concepts.misconception: Reading 4 × 6 as "4 plus 6", or seeing division only as sharing and missing the how-many-groups meaning.
concepts.supports: Sentence frame: "___ groups of ___ is ___." Start with factors of 2, 5 and 10 before 6-9.

NC.prompt: Ms. Bell puts 24 crayons into 4 boxes with the same number in each box. Draw a model. Write a multiplication equation and a division equation for the crayons.
NC.answer: 6 crayons in each box. 4 × 6 = 24 and 24 ÷ 4 = 6.

MI.prompt: A teacher sets up 5 rows of chairs with 3 chairs in each row. Select all expressions that show the total number of chairs.

TX.prompt: Rosa has 32 stickers. She puts them in groups of 4. Which equation can be used to find g, the number of groups?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Properties & fact fluency within 100
concepts.summary: Use commutative, associative and distributive properties and the multiplication-division relationship to know facts to 10 × 10.
steps: Anchor facts: ×2, ×5, ×10 through skip counting and doubles.
Rotate arrays to prove turnaround facts (3 × 8 = 8 × 3).
Break apart arrays to derive harder facts: 7 × 8 = 5 × 8 + 2 × 8.
Build fact families that link each multiplication fact to two division facts.
Fluency practice with strategy talk ("How did you get it?") rather than speed alone.
concepts.check: You know 5 × 7 = 35. Use it to find 6 × 7 and explain with a drawing.
concepts.misconception: Applying the commutative property to division or subtraction (12 ÷ 3 = 3 ÷ 12).
concepts.supports: Fact strategy cards with array pictures; let students self-track which facts are known vs. derived.

NC.prompt: Use a fact you know to solve 7 × 8. Show your strategy with an array or equations.

MI.prompt: Find the missing number: 6 × ☐ = 54. Then write a division fact from the same fact family.

TX.prompt: Which expression has the same value as 9 × 6?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Two-step problems & arithmetic patterns
concepts.summary: Solve two-step problems with all four operations, represent them with equations using a letter for the unknown, and check reasonableness.
steps: Retell the problem with no numbers: what is happening?
Find the hidden first question that must be answered before the main one.
Model both steps with a strip (bar) diagram.
Write one equation with a letter for the unknown.
Estimate first, then compare the answer to the estimate.
concepts.check: A class has 4 packs of 8 markers and gives away 9. How many are left? Show the hidden question.
concepts.misconception: Grabbing every number and adding them; skipping the first step.
concepts.supports: Read-draw-write routine; visual problem mats with two boxes for step 1 and step 2.

NC.prompt: The library had 135 books. It got 3 boxes with 8 books in each box. Write an equation with a letter for the unknown, then solve.

MI.prompt: Jamal had $45. He spent $18 on a game and split the rest equally into 3 jars. How much money is in each jar? Use estimation to explain why your answer is reasonable.
MI.answer: $9. 45 − 18 = 27 and 27 ÷ 3 = 9. Estimate: 50 − 20 = 30 and 30 ÷ 3 = 10, which is close to 9.

TX.prompt: A farmer planted 6 rows of tomato plants with 7 plants in each row. Then 9 plants died. How many tomato plants are left?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Place value, rounding & add/subtract within 1,000
concepts.summary: Round to the nearest 10 or 100 and add and subtract fluently within 1,000 using place-value strategies. Texas extends place value to 100,000.
steps: Build numbers with base-ten blocks and trade 10 ones for 1 ten.
Record on place-value charts and in expanded form.
Round on a vertical number line: which ten or hundred is closer?
Add and subtract with partial sums and open number lines.
Connect each step of the standard algorithm to the blocks.
concepts.check: Round 467 to the nearest ten and hundred, and show both on a number line.
concepts.misconception: Rounding by changing digits without knowing which benchmark is closer; subtracting the smaller digit from the larger in every column.
concepts.supports: Keep blocks available during the algorithm; color-code place values.

NC.prompt: Round 638 to the nearest ten and to the nearest hundred. Show both on a number line.
NC.answer: Nearest ten: 640. Nearest hundred: 600.

MI.prompt: Select all numbers that round to 500 when rounded to the nearest hundred.

TX.prompt: Students collected 47,385 cans. What is the value of the digit 7 in 47,385?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Unit fractions & fractions on a number line
concepts.summary: Understand 1/b as one of b equal parts, build fractions from unit fractions and place them on a number line.
steps: Fold paper strips into equal parts and name one part.
Name the unit fraction: 1/b is one of b equal parts of the whole.
Count unit fractions: 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 4/4.
Partition 0 to 1 on a number line and label each point.
Extend past 1 and connect 4/4 to 1 whole.
concepts.check: Mark 3/4 on a number line from 0 to 2 and explain how you found the spot.
concepts.misconception: Believing a bigger denominator means a bigger piece; counting tick marks instead of spaces.
concepts.supports: Fraction strips taped above the number line so both models stay visible.

NC.prompt: Partition a number line from 0 to 1 into sixths. Label 1/6 and 5/6. How many sixths make 1 whole?
NC.answer: Six equal spaces; 1/6 is the first mark, 5/6 the fifth; 6/6 = 1.

MI.prompt: A number line from 0 to 1 is split into 4 equal parts. Point P is on the third mark after 0. What fraction does P show? Explain.
MI.answer: 3/4. Each space is 1/4 and P is 3 spaces from 0.

TX.prompt: A strip is divided into 8 equal parts and 3 parts are shaded. Which fraction is shaded?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Equivalent & comparing fractions
concepts.summary: Explain equivalence with models and compare fractions with the same numerator or the same denominator.
steps: Lay fraction strips side by side to find pieces that cover the same length.
Show equivalent fractions at the same point on a number line.
Write whole numbers as fractions (3 = 3/1, 1 = 4/4).
Compare same-denominator fractions by counting pieces.
Compare same-numerator fractions by reasoning about piece size.
concepts.check: Which is greater, 2/3 or 2/6? Explain without drawing the same-size whole incorrectly.
concepts.misconception: Comparing fractions whose wholes are different sizes.
concepts.supports: Always draw the wholes the same size; use the language "same size pieces".

NC.prompt: Use fraction strips to show that 2/4 = 1/2. Then name a fraction equal to 1/2 that has a denominator of 8.

MI.prompt: Compare 3/8 and 3/4 using >, <, or =. Explain with a drawing.
MI.answer: 3/8 < 3/4. Both have 3 pieces, but eighths are smaller pieces than fourths.

TX.prompt: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/3?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Area & its link to multiplication
concepts.summary: Measure area by counting unit squares, relate tiling to multiplication, and find areas of rectilinear figures by decomposing.
steps: Cover rectangles with square tiles with no gaps or overlaps.
Draw the grid in rows and columns and count by rows.
Replace counting with multiplication: rows × columns.
Split an L-shape into two rectangles and add the areas.
Use an area model to show 6 × 7 = 6 × 5 + 6 × 2.
concepts.check: Find the area of an L-shaped garden two different ways.
concepts.misconception: Mixing up area and perimeter; counting tick marks along edges.
concepts.supports: Grid paper overlays; word wall with "square units" vs "units".

NC.prompt: A rug is 6 feet long and 4 feet wide. Find its area by tiling and by multiplying.
NC.answer: 24 square feet

MI.prompt: An L-shaped room is made of a 5 m by 3 m rectangle and a 2 m by 2 m rectangle. What is the total area? Show how you split the shape.
MI.answer: 15 + 4 = 19 square meters

TX.prompt: A rectangle has an area of 36 square units. Its length is 9 units. What is its width?
TX.answer: 4 units

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Perimeter
concepts.summary: Find perimeters of polygons, including an unknown side, and compare rectangles with the same perimeter or area.
steps: Walk the edge of a shape on the floor and count steps.
Trace edges on grid paper and label each side length.
Add side lengths; find a missing side when the total is known.
Build rectangles with the same area and different perimeters.
concepts.check: A rectangle has perimeter 18 cm and one side of 5 cm. Find the other sides.
concepts.misconception: Counting squares inside a shape when asked for perimeter.
concepts.supports: Highlight edges in one color and interiors in another.

NC.prompt: A rectangular garden is 7 feet long and 3 feet wide. What is its perimeter?
NC.answer: 20 feet

MI.prompt: Draw two different rectangles that each have an area of 12 square units. Find the perimeter of each.
MI.answer: Example: 2 × 6 has perimeter 16; 3 × 4 has perimeter 14.

TX.prompt: A triangle has a perimeter of 24 centimeters. Two sides are 8 cm and 9 cm. How long is the third side, in centimeters?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Time, mass & liquid volume
concepts.summary: Tell time to the minute and solve elapsed-time problems; measure and estimate liquid volume and mass.
steps: Read analog clocks to the minute.
Model elapsed time on an open number line (jump to the hour, then minutes).
Estimate and measure liquid volume with liters and mass with grams and kilograms.
Solve one-step word problems with these measurements.
concepts.check: Recess starts at 10:47 and ends at 11:15. How long is recess? Show your number line.
concepts.misconception: Treating time as base ten (10:50 + 20 min = 10:70).
concepts.supports: Clock manipulatives; real containers and scales.

NC.prompt: Soccer practice starts at 3:45 p.m. and ends at 4:30 p.m. Use a number line to find how long practice lasts.
NC.answer: 45 minutes

MI.prompt: Would you measure the water in a bathtub in milliliters or liters? Explain your choice.
MI.answer: Liters, because a bathtub holds a large amount of water.

TX.prompt: Recess started at 11:25 a.m. and lasted 35 minutes. What time did recess end?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Scaled picture graphs, bar graphs & line plots
concepts.summary: Draw and read scaled graphs and answer one- and two-step how-many-more questions; make line plots of measurement data.
steps: Collect class data and sort it into categories.
Make a picture graph where each picture stands for 2 or 5.
Turn it into a bar graph with a scaled axis.
Ask and answer how-many-more and how-many-fewer questions.
concepts.check: On a bar graph scaled by 5s, how many more students chose soccer than tennis?
concepts.misconception: Reading the scale as 1 per gridline.
concepts.supports: Color the scale labels; start with familiar data like class favorites.

NC.prompt: In a picture graph, each ☺ = 2 students. Pizza has 6 ☺ and tacos has 4 ☺. How many more students chose pizza than tacos?
NC.answer: 12 − 8 = 4 more students

MI.prompt: Make a bar graph with a scale of 5: Dogs 25, Cats 15, Fish 10. How many fewer students chose fish than dogs?
MI.answer: 15 fewer

TX.prompt: A bar graph with a scale of 10 shows votes: Red 40, Blue 25, Green 35. How many students voted in all?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Classify quadrilaterals & partition shapes
concepts.summary: Sort shapes by attributes, recognize categories of quadrilaterals and partition shapes into equal-area parts.
steps: Sort a mixed set of shapes and name the sorting rule.
Find the attributes all quadrilaterals share.
Sort quadrilaterals into rhombuses, rectangles and squares and find overlaps.
Partition shapes into equal-area parts and name each part as a unit fraction.
concepts.check: Draw a quadrilateral that is not a rhombus, rectangle or square.
concepts.misconception: Thinking a square is not a rectangle; judging shapes by orientation.
concepts.supports: Venn diagrams with physical shapes students can move.

NC.prompt: Draw a quadrilateral that is not a rectangle, a square or a rhombus. Name it and explain why it belongs in the quadrilateral group.
NC.answer: Example: a trapezoid. It has 4 sides and 4 angles.

MI.prompt: Select all shapes that are always quadrilaterals.
MI.answer: square, rhombus, trapezoid

TX.prompt: Which figure has 4 sides and 4 right angles but sides that are not all the same length?
TX.answer: rectangle

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Personal financial literacy
concepts.summary: Connect work to income, explain scarcity and cost, compare planned and unplanned spending, saving and credit.
steps: Discuss jobs and the skills that earn income.
Role-play a store with limited items to show scarcity and cost.
Plan a budget and compare with an unplanned purchase.
Explain saving and lending with simple stories.
concepts.check: Explain why a scarce toy might cost more.
concepts.misconception: Believing credit is free money.
concepts.supports: Classroom economy or play-money simulation.

TX.prompt: Ana planned to spend $5 on lunch. At the store she also bought a $2 snack she had not planned on. Which statement is true?
choices: The snack was unplanned spending, so Ana has $2 less to save.
Unplanned spending always costs more than planned spending.
Ana used credit to buy the snack.
TX.answer: The snack was unplanned spending, so Ana has $2 less to save.

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Place value & rounding to 1,000,000
concepts.summary: Recognize that a digit is 10 times what it represents to its right; read, write, compare and round multi-digit whole numbers.
steps: Build 1, 10, 100, 1,000 with blocks and name the times-ten pattern.
Write numbers in standard, word and expanded form.
Compare numbers with place-value charts and symbols.
Round to any place using a number line and benchmarks.
concepts.check: How is the 4 in 4,000 related to the 4 in 400?
concepts.misconception: Comparing by the first digit regardless of number length.
concepts.supports: Place-value chart with period commas; read numbers aloud by periods.

NC.prompt: How does the value of the 3 in 35,000 compare to the value of the 3 in 3,500?
NC.answer: It is 10 times as much (30,000 vs 3,000).

MI.prompt: Round 268,451 to the nearest thousand.

TX.prompt: Which shows 504,230 in expanded notation?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Fluent multi-digit addition & subtraction
concepts.summary: Add and subtract multi-digit whole numbers with the standard algorithm. Texas also includes decimals to hundredths.
steps: Review partial sums and differences with blocks.
Link each regroup in the algorithm to a block trade.
Subtract across zeros by regrouping from the next nonzero place.
Estimate first and check with the inverse operation.
concepts.check: Solve 6,003 − 2,478 and check by adding.
concepts.misconception: Regrouping errors across zeros; misaligned columns.
concepts.supports: Graph paper for column alignment; worked examples with one error to find.

NC.prompt: Solve 6,003 − 2,478 with the standard algorithm. Check your answer with addition.

MI.prompt: A stadium had 45,672 fans on Friday and 38,915 fans on Saturday. How many more fans came on Friday?

TX.prompt: Mia ran 2.75 miles on Monday and 1.6 miles on Tuesday. How many miles did she run in all?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Multiplicative comparison & multi-digit multiplication
concepts.summary: Interpret "times as many" comparisons and multiply up to 4-digit by 1-digit and 2-digit by 2-digit numbers using place-value strategies.
steps: Model "3 times as many" with comparison strip diagrams.
Multiply by 10 and 100 and explain the place-value shift.
Use area models to multiply 2-digit by 2-digit (four partial products).
Record partial products, then compress to the standard algorithm.
Estimate products by rounding to check reasonableness.
concepts.check: Use an area model to solve 23 × 46 and connect each part to the algorithm.
concepts.misconception: Treating comparison as additive (3 times as many as 5 = 8); dropping the zero in 20 × 6.
concepts.supports: Area-model templates; color each partial product.

NC.prompt: Use an area model and partial products to solve 34 × 26.

MI.prompt: A whale is 8 times as long as a dolphin. The dolphin is 6 feet long. Write an equation and find the whale's length.
MI.answer: 8 × 6 = w; w = 48 feet

TX.prompt: A theater has 24 rows with 35 seats in each row. How many seats are in the theater?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Division with remainders
concepts.summary: Find quotients up to 4-digit dividends and 1-digit divisors and interpret remainders in context.
steps: Share base-ten blocks equally and trade when stuck.
Use an area model with a missing side length.
Record partial quotients ("How many groups can I take out?").
Decide what the remainder means: drop it, round up or report it.
Check by multiplying and adding the remainder.
concepts.check: 25 students ride in vans that hold 6. How many vans are needed? Explain the remainder.
concepts.misconception: Ignoring the context of the remainder; remainder larger than the divisor.
concepts.supports: Remainder decision chart with three picture examples.

NC.prompt: 53 students are going on a field trip. Each van holds 7 students. How many vans are needed? Explain what the remainder means.
NC.answer: 53 ÷ 7 = 7 R4, so 8 vans. The 4 extra students still need a van.

MI.prompt: Use partial quotients to solve 1,248 ÷ 4.

TX.prompt: Mr. Lee shares 196 markers equally among 8 tables. How many markers does each table get, and how many are left over?
TX.answer: 24, with 4 left over

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Factors, multiples & patterns
concepts.summary: Find factor pairs to 100, identify prime and composite numbers and generate patterns from a rule.
steps: Build all rectangles with 12 tiles to find its factor pairs.
Sort numbers by how many rectangles they make (prime vs composite).
Generate a pattern from a rule and look for features the rule does not state.
Use input-output tables to describe a rule.
concepts.check: Is 51 prime or composite? Prove it.
concepts.misconception: Calling 1 prime; confusing factors and multiples.
concepts.supports: Hundreds-chart sieve activity. Texas formally teaches prime and composite in grade 5 (5.4A).

NC.prompt: List all factor pairs of 36. Is 36 prime or composite? Explain.
NC.answer: 1 × 36, 2 × 18, 3 × 12, 4 × 9, 6 × 6. Composite, because it has more than two factors.

MI.prompt: Select all numbers that are multiples of 6.

TX.prompt: An input-output table shows 2 → 10, 4 → 20, 6 → 30, 8 → 40. Which rule describes the table?
TX.answer: Multiply by 5

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Equivalent fractions & comparing
concepts.summary: Explain why multiplying numerator and denominator by the same number makes an equivalent fraction; compare fractions with unlike denominators.
steps: Split each piece of a fraction strip again and name the new fraction.
Describe the pattern: n × a / n × b.
Compare to benchmarks 0, 1/2 and 1.
Rename to a common denominator or numerator to compare.
concepts.check: Order 3/8, 2/3 and 1/2 and explain using a benchmark.
concepts.misconception: Comparing numerators and denominators separately (3/8 > 2/3 because 8 > 3).
concepts.supports: Benchmark number line on desk; fraction tiles.

NC.prompt: Use an area model to show why 2/3 = 8/12.
NC.answer: Split each third into 4 equal parts: 2 × 4 = 8 shaded out of 3 × 4 = 12.

MI.prompt: Compare 5/8 and 3/4. Explain using a common denominator or a benchmark.

TX.prompt: Which fraction is greater than 1/2?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Add & subtract fractions; fraction times whole number
concepts.summary: Decompose fractions into unit fractions, add and subtract like denominators and mixed numbers, and multiply a fraction by a whole number (NC, MI).
steps: Decompose 5/6 as 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 and in other ways.
Add and subtract like denominators on a number line.
Rename mixed numbers to add and subtract them.
Model 3 × 2/5 as 3 groups of 2/5 (NC, MI).
concepts.check: Show 2 1/4 − 3/4 on a number line.
concepts.misconception: Adding denominators (1/4 + 2/4 = 3/8).
concepts.supports: Say the unit aloud: "one fourth plus two fourths is three fourths". Texas multiplies a fraction by a whole number in grade 5 (5.3I).

NC.prompt: Mrs. Jones has 2 3/8 pizzas. Her class eats 1 5/8 pizzas. How much pizza is left?
NC.answer: 6/8 (or 3/4) of a pizza

MI.prompt: Write 5/6 as a sum of fractions with the same denominator in two different ways.

TX.prompt: Kai walked 3/10 mile in the morning and 5/10 mile in the afternoon. How far did he walk in all?
TX.answer: 8/10 mile

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Decimals to hundredths
concepts.summary: Write tenths and hundredths as decimals, relate them to fractions and money, and compare decimals.
steps: Shade tenths and hundredths grids; rename 3/10 as 30/100.
Connect to money: dimes and pennies.
Place decimals on a number line from 0 to 1.
Compare decimals with grids and place-value charts.
concepts.check: Which is greater, 0.5 or 0.45? Show with a grid.
concepts.misconception: Thinking longer decimals are larger (0.45 > 0.5).
concepts.supports: Decimal grids and money; always say "five tenths" instead of "point five".

NC.prompt: Write 47/100 as a decimal and shade it on a hundredths grid.

MI.prompt: Select all comparisons that are true.

TX.prompt: A number line from 0 to 1 is divided into tenths. Point P is on the seventh mark. Which decimal names point P?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Lines, angles & symmetry
concepts.summary: Draw and identify lines, rays and angles; measure angles with a protractor; classify figures by parallel and perpendicular sides and angles; find lines of symmetry.
steps: Model rays and angles with arms or straws.
Compare angles to a right-angle corner (smaller, equal, larger).
Treat an angle as a turn: 1/360 of a circle is 1 degree.
Measure and draw angles with a protractor; find missing angles by addition.
Classify triangles and quadrilaterals by angles and parallel or perpendicular sides.
concepts.check: Two angles together make a right angle. One is 35°. Find the other.
concepts.misconception: Reading the wrong protractor scale; thinking longer rays make bigger angles.
concepts.supports: Paper protractors with one scale highlighted.

NC.prompt: Two angles together form a right angle. One angle measures 38°. What is the measure of the other angle?

MI.prompt: Draw a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides and two right angles. Mark the parallel sides.
MI.answer: A right trapezoid.

TX.prompt: Which kind of triangle has one angle that measures more than 90°?
TX.answer: obtuse

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Measurement conversions, area & perimeter formulas
concepts.summary: Convert larger units to smaller ones and apply area and perimeter formulas for rectangles.
steps: Make conversion tables (1 ft = 12 in, 2 ft = 24 in...).
Solve measurement word problems with strip diagrams.
Derive A = l × w and P = 2l + 2w from grids.
Find an unknown side from a known area or perimeter.
concepts.check: A rug is 3 ft by 5 ft. What is its area in square inches?
concepts.misconception: Dividing instead of multiplying when converting to smaller units.
concepts.supports: Two-column conversion charts; real rulers and yardsticks.

NC.prompt: A rectangle has a perimeter of 30 cm and a length of 9 cm. Find its width and its area.
NC.answer: Width 6 cm; area 54 square cm

MI.prompt: Complete the table: 1 foot = 12 inches; 3 feet = ☐ inches; 5 feet = ☐ inches.

TX.prompt: A board is 4 yards long. How many feet long is the board?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Line plots with fractions
concepts.summary: Make line plots of measurements in fractions of a unit and solve problems with the data.
steps: Measure objects to the nearest 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 inch.
Build a line plot with fractional tick marks.
Answer questions that need adding or subtracting the fractions.
concepts.check: What is the difference between the longest and shortest pencil on the plot?
concepts.misconception: Unequal spacing between fraction marks.
concepts.supports: Pre-marked number lines for the first plots.

NC.prompt: A line plot shows ribbon lengths: 1/4, 1/2, 1/2, 3/4, 3/4, 3/4 inch. What is the difference between the longest and shortest ribbon?
NC.answer: 1/2 inch

MI.prompt: Using the same line plot, what is the total length of all the 3/4-inch ribbons?
MI.answer: 9/4 = 2 1/4 inches

TX.prompt: A stem-and-leaf plot shows 2 | 3 5 8 and 3 | 0 4. What is the difference between the greatest and least values?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Personal financial literacy
concepts.summary: Distinguish fixed and variable expenses, calculate profit, compare saving options, and describe budgets and financial institutions.
steps: Sort household expenses as fixed or variable.
Calculate profit for a lemonade stand.
Compare saving at home vs at a bank.
Build a simple budget.
concepts.check: A stand earns $45 and spends $18. What is the profit?
concepts.misconception: Confusing revenue with profit.
concepts.supports: Use classroom-business simulations.

TX.prompt: A lemonade stand earned $36. The supplies cost $14. What was the profit, in dollars?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Decimal place value to thousandths
concepts.summary: Understand that each place is 10 times the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left; read, write, compare and round decimals.
steps: Extend the place-value chart to thousandths with base-ten models.
Show multiplying and dividing by 10, 100, 1,000 as moving digits.
Write decimals in expanded form, including fraction form.
Compare and round decimals on number lines.
concepts.check: Round 4.376 to the nearest tenth and hundredth.
concepts.misconception: Thinking 0.125 > 0.13 because it has more digits.
concepts.supports: Hundredths and thousandths grids; place-value sliders.

NC.prompt: Write 3.507 in expanded form.

MI.prompt: Explain why 4.3 × 10 = 43 using place value.
MI.answer: Each digit becomes 10 times as large and moves one place to the left.

TX.prompt: Which decimal rounds to 6.4 when rounded to the nearest tenth?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Multi-digit multiplication & division
concepts.summary: Multiply fluently with the standard algorithm and divide up to 4-digit dividends by 2-digit divisors.
steps: Review area models and partial products.
Move to the standard algorithm and name each partial product.
Divide by 2-digit divisors with partial quotients and estimation.
Compare strategies and check with the inverse.
concepts.check: Solve 1,428 ÷ 34 two ways.
concepts.misconception: Underestimating partial quotients and getting stuck.
concepts.supports: Multiples list for the divisor at the top of the page.

NC.prompt: Solve 1,512 ÷ 24 using partial quotients. Check with multiplication.

MI.prompt: A school orders 215 boxes of pencils with 36 pencils in each box. How many pencils is that?

TX.prompt: A factory packs 2,856 cans into boxes of 24. How many boxes does it fill?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Operations with decimals
concepts.summary: Add, subtract, multiply and divide decimals to hundredths using models, place value and properties.
steps: Add and subtract decimals with grids, lining up like places.
Model 0.3 × 0.4 with an area model on a hundredths grid.
Model division of decimals as equal groups of hundredths.
Use estimation to place the decimal point and check.
concepts.check: Explain why 0.3 × 0.4 is 0.12 and not 1.2.
concepts.misconception: Lining up the last digits instead of the places; expecting multiplication to always make bigger.
concepts.supports: Decimal grids; estimation before computation every time.

NC.prompt: Use a hundredths grid to show 0.4 × 0.6.

MI.prompt: Sam buys 3 notebooks for $2.45 each and pays with a $10 bill. How much change does he get?

TX.prompt: A ribbon 4.8 meters long is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each piece, in meters?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Add & subtract fractions with unlike denominators
concepts.summary: Replace fractions with equivalent fractions to add and subtract, including mixed numbers, and judge reasonableness with benchmarks.
steps: Model 1/2 + 1/3 with fraction strips and find a common piece size.
Use area models to find common denominators.
Add and subtract mixed numbers, regrouping when needed.
Estimate with benchmarks (1/2 + 3/8 is a little less than 1).
concepts.check: Is 2/3 + 1/4 more or less than 1? Prove it, then compute.
concepts.misconception: Adding numerators and denominators (1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5).
concepts.supports: Fraction-strip kits; benchmark number line.

NC.prompt: Find 2/3 + 1/4. Use an area model to find a common denominator.

MI.prompt: Maria says 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5. Is she correct? Use a benchmark to explain, then find the correct sum.
MI.answer: No. 2/5 is less than 1/2, so it can't be the sum. 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6.

TX.prompt: Jada used 3 1/2 cups of flour and 1 2/3 cups of sugar. How much more flour than sugar did she use?
TX.answer: 1 5/6 cups

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Multiply fractions & fractions as division
concepts.summary: Interpret a/b as a ÷ b, multiply fractions and whole numbers by fractions, and reason about scaling.
steps: Share 3 sandwiches among 4 people to see 3 ÷ 4 = 3/4.
Model a fraction of a whole number with equal groups.
Use area models to multiply fraction by fraction.
Predict whether a product will be larger or smaller than a factor (scaling).
concepts.check: Without computing, is 7/8 × 15 more or less than 15? Why?
concepts.misconception: Believing multiplication always makes a number bigger.
concepts.supports: Area-model grids. Texas limits grade 5 to whole number × fraction (5.3I).

NC.prompt: Use an area model to find 2/3 × 3/4.

MI.prompt: Without calculating, is 5/6 × 12 greater than or less than 12? Explain.
MI.answer: Less, because 12 is multiplied by a fraction less than 1.

TX.prompt: A recipe uses 3/4 cup of milk for each batch. How many cups of milk are needed for 6 batches?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Divide with unit fractions
concepts.summary: Divide unit fractions by whole numbers and whole numbers by unit fractions using models.
steps: Ask "how many 1/3s are in 2?" and model with strips.
Model 1/3 ÷ 4 as sharing one-third into 4 equal parts.
Write the matching multiplication equation to check.
Solve word problems and decide which division meaning fits.
concepts.check: How many 1/4-cup servings are in 3 cups? Draw it.
concepts.misconception: Dividing the wrong number by the other; expecting the quotient to be smaller.
concepts.supports: Measuring cups for real-world modeling.

NC.prompt: How many 1/3-cup servings are in 4 cups of trail mix? Draw a model.
NC.answer: 12 servings; 4 ÷ 1/3 = 12

MI.prompt: Four friends share 1/2 pound of fudge equally. How much does each friend get? Draw a model.

TX.prompt: What is the value of 5 ÷ 1/4?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Numerical expressions, patterns & prime numbers
concepts.summary: Write and evaluate expressions with parentheses, generate two related patterns and graph the pairs. Texas adds prime and composite numbers.
steps: Translate words into expressions ("three times the sum of 5 and 2").
Evaluate expressions with grouping symbols.
Generate two patterns from rules and compare corresponding terms.
Graph the ordered pairs and describe the relationship.
concepts.check: Write an expression for "double 8, then add 7" and another for "add 8 and 7, then double". Compare.
concepts.misconception: Working strictly left to right and ignoring grouping symbols.
concepts.supports: Color-code grouping symbols; expression-to-words matching cards.

NC.prompt: Evaluate 3 × (12 − 4) + 6.

MI.prompt: Write an expression for "add 7 and 5, then multiply by 4." Without calculating, compare its value with 7 + 5.
MI.answer: (7 + 5) × 4; it is 4 times as large as 7 + 5.

TX.prompt: Which number is prime?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Coordinate plane
concepts.summary: Graph points in the first quadrant and interpret coordinates in real-world problems.
steps: Build two perpendicular number lines on the floor.
Walk to points: over on x, then up on y.
Plot points from a table of values.
Interpret points in a context (time and distance).
concepts.check: Plot (3, 5) and (5, 3). Why are they different points?
concepts.misconception: Reversing x and y.
concepts.supports: Mnemonic: "run before you jump". Floor grid with tape.

NC.prompt: Plot (2, 5) and (5, 2) on a coordinate plane. Explain why they are different points.
NC.answer: The first number is the distance along the x-axis and the second is along the y-axis, so switching them changes the location.

MI.prompt: Rule A: start at 0 and add 2. Rule B: start at 0 and add 6. Write the first four ordered pairs (A, B) and describe the relationship.
MI.answer: (0, 0), (2, 6), (4, 12), (6, 18). Each B term is 3 times the A term.

TX.prompt: Point A is 4 units to the right of the origin and 7 units up. Which ordered pair names point A?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Volume of rectangular prisms
concepts.summary: Understand volume as unit cubes, use l × w × h and B × h, and add volumes of composite figures.
steps: Pack boxes with unit cubes and count.
Count layers: area of the base times the number of layers.
Generalize to V = l × w × h and V = B × h.
Find volumes of composite figures by adding.
concepts.check: A box has a base of 12 cubes and is 5 layers tall. What is its volume?
concepts.misconception: Confusing surface area or area with volume; using square units.
concepts.supports: Snap cubes and nets of boxes.

NC.prompt: A box has a base of 4 cm by 3 cm and a height of 5 cm. Find its volume by thinking in layers.
NC.answer: 12 cubes per layer × 5 layers = 60 cubic cm

MI.prompt: A figure is made of a 5 × 2 × 3 prism and a 2 × 2 × 3 prism that do not overlap. What is the total volume?
MI.answer: 30 + 12 = 42 cubic units

TX.prompt: A rectangular prism has a volume of 96 cubic inches, a length of 4 inches and a width of 3 inches. What is its height, in inches?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Classify 2D figures in a hierarchy
concepts.summary: Classify two-dimensional figures in a hierarchy based on their properties.
steps: Sort shapes by side and angle properties.
Build a hierarchy diagram for quadrilaterals.
Use "all, some, none" statements to justify placements.
concepts.check: True or false: all rhombuses are parallelograms. Justify.
concepts.misconception: Treating categories as exclusive (a square is not a rhombus).
concepts.supports: Nested-box graphic organizer.

NC.prompt: True or false: every square is a rhombus. Explain using properties.
NC.answer: True. A square has 4 equal sides, which is the property that defines a rhombus.

MI.prompt: Select all statements that are always true.
MI.answer: A rectangle is a parallelogram; A square is a rectangle.

TX.prompt: Which category includes squares, rectangles and rhombuses?
TX.answer: parallelograms

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Unit conversions & line plots
concepts.summary: Convert units within a system in multi-step problems and use line plots of fractional data. Texas adds stem-and-leaf plots and scatterplots.
steps: Build metric conversion charts tied to place value.
Solve multi-step conversion problems.
Create line plots of fractional measurements and redistribute evenly.
Interpret other data displays (TX: stem-and-leaf, scatterplot).
concepts.check: Convert 3.5 kg to grams and explain using place value.
concepts.misconception: Multiplying when they should divide in conversions.
concepts.supports: Metric staircase visual.

NC.prompt: Use a conversion chart to convert 3.5 kilometers to meters.
NC.answer: 3,500 meters

MI.prompt: A line plot shows 4 beakers holding 1/4, 1/2, 1/2 and 3/4 liter. If the water were shared equally, how much would each beaker hold?
MI.answer: Total 2 liters ÷ 4 = 1/2 liter

TX.prompt: A rope is 5 yards long. How many feet long is it?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Personal financial literacy
concepts.summary: Define taxes, compare payment methods, balance a budget and describe gross and net income.
steps: Sort taxes (income, payroll, sales, property).
Compare cash, debit, credit and electronic payments.
Find net income from gross income and deductions.
Balance a simple budget.
concepts.check: A paycheck is $600 with $90 withheld. What is net income?
concepts.misconception: Thinking gross pay is what you take home.
concepts.supports: Budget simulations with realistic local prices.

TX.prompt: Ms. Cruz has a gross income of $2,400 per month. $360 is withheld for taxes. What is her net income, in dollars?

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Count to 100 & write numbers to 20
concepts.summary: Count to 100 by ones and tens, count forward from any number, and write numbers 0 to 20.
prereqs: PreK: Say the counting sequence to 10 or more
steps: Count real objects every day (lunch count, steps to the door).
Count along a hundred chart, pointing to each number.
Count by tens with ten-frames and bundles of ten sticks.
Start counting from a number other than 1 ("start at 7").
Write numerals 0 to 20 to label sets.
concepts.check: Start at 8 and count to 15. Then write the number 15.
concepts.misconception: Skipping the teens or saying "tenty" after 19; reversing written digits (writing 12 as 21).
concepts.supports: Number lines and hundred charts at every table; counting songs that cross decades (28, 29, 30).

NC.prompt: Start at 18 and count to 25. Then write the number that comes after 19.

MI.prompt: Start at 18 and count to 25. Then write the number that comes after 19.

TX.prompt: Start at 18 and count to 25. Then write the number that comes after 19.

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Count to tell how many
concepts.summary: Match one number to one object, know the last number said tells how many, and see small amounts at a glance.
steps: Touch and move each object as you count it.
Ask "How many?" after counting; answer with the last number said.
Flash dot cards and ten-frames to subitize up to 5, then 10.
Make a set one more and one less than a number.
Count up to 20 objects in a line, array or circle, and up to 10 scattered.
concepts.check: Here are 9 counters scattered. How many? Now make a group with one more.
concepts.misconception: Counting an object twice or skipping one; recounting from 1 instead of trusting the last number.
concepts.supports: Counting mats with a start dot; five-frames before ten-frames.

NC.prompt: Count these stars: ★★★★★★★. How many stars? Draw one more. How many now?
NC.answer: 7 stars; with one more there are 8.

MI.prompt: Count these stars: ★★★★★★★. How many stars? Draw one more. How many now?
MI.answer: 7 stars; with one more there are 8.

TX.prompt: Count these stars: ★★★★★★★. How many stars? Draw one more. How many now?
TX.answer: 7 stars; with one more there are 8.

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Compare numbers & groups
concepts.summary: Decide whether one group has more, fewer or the same as another, and compare numerals 1 to 10.
steps: Line up two sets of cubes side by side and match them one to one.

concepts.subject: math

Find patterns on the 120 chart.
Count large collections by grouping into tens.
Write numbers to 120 to label collections.

concepts.misconception: Saying "one hundred ten" for 101 or writing 100 + 1 as 1001.

concepts.subject: math
concepts.name: Add within 100; 10 more & 10 less
concepts.summary: Add a two-digit and a one-digit number or a multiple of 10 using place value, and find 10 more or 10 less mentally.
steps: Use base-ten blocks: add tens to tens and ones to ones.

Move up and down a column on the hundred chart for 10 more and 10 less.

concepts.subject: math

Read hour and half-hour times on an analog clock.
Match analog and digital times.

Ask how many in all and how many more.

NC.prompt: How does Lila feel when she opens her jar of seeds? Use two details from the story to explain how you know.
NC.answer: Upset or disappointed. She says, "They're ruined," and "Her chin wobbled."

MI.prompt: Part A: Why does Mr. Okafor give Lila an envelope of seeds? Part B: Which sentence from the story best supports your answer to Part A?

He wants to thank her for her hard work.
He has no room left for his seeds.

Lila sat on the steps while neighbors traded.
Lila counted carefully, ten seeds in each envelope.
That night, Lila wrote a label for a new jar: DRY FIRST.

Track what the main character learns or how they change.
Turn the lesson into a statement that applies to anyone.

Compare themes across two texts.
concepts.check: State the theme of a fable in a full sentence and give two details that support it.

NC.prompt: What is the central message of "The Seed Swap"? Explain how Lila's actions show this message.
NC.answer: Example: A mistake can teach you something, and you can still find a way to help. Lila helps Mr. Okafor and learns to dry her seeds first.

MI.prompt: Part A: Which statement best describes the central message of the story? Part B: Which detail best supports your answer?

MI.answer: Part A: When something goes wrong, you can still learn and help others. Part B: Lila helps count seeds and writes DRY FIRST on a new jar.

TX.prompt: What lesson does Lila learn in "The Seed Swap"? Use evidence from the story to support your answer.

She trades the moldy seeds for pepper seeds.
She tells Lila to go inside.
TX.answer: She explains why the seeds got moldy and how to save them next time.

Burdock seeds are covered in tiny hooks.
A coconut has a hard, waterproof shell, so it can drift across the ocean.

TX.prompt: Why does the author include the last paragraph?

To tell a story about a dog
TX.answer: To explain why it helps plants when seeds spread out

Use the new word in speaking and writing.

MI.answer: Part A: to catch or get. Part B: "the hooks catch its fur."

TX.prompt: In the story, Lila "counted carefully." The suffix -ly in carefully tells —

TX.answer: sky / by

MI.prompt: Which structure does the author mainly use in paragraphs 3 and 4?

TX.prompt: Why does the author include the statistic "1 in 1,000 hatchlings survives" in the last paragraph?

To explain why every protected nest matters
To describe what a nest looks like

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Vocabulary in context
concepts.summary: Determine meanings of words using context, affixes, roots and reference materials. Grade focus: Use context, Greek and Latin affixes and roots.
steps: Model a think-aloud with context clues.
Teach a context clue type (definition, example, contrast).
Break words into prefix, root and suffix.
Confirm meaning with a dictionary or glossary.
Use the new word in speaking and writing.
concepts.check: Figure out the meaning of an unfamiliar word in a passage and explain the clue you used.
concepts.misconception: Guessing from the first letter; ignoring sentences around the word.
concepts.supports: Affix word walls; picture glossaries for ELLs.

NC.prompt: Use context to determine the meaning of instinct in paragraph 3 of the article. Which clues helped?
NC.answer: A natural behavior an animal is born with. Paragraph 2 explains hatchlings crawl toward the brightest horizon without being taught.

MI.prompt: Part A: What does predators mean in paragraph 2? Part B: Which sentence helps you understand it?
MI.answer: Part A: animals that hunt other animals. Part B: "Ghost crabs and birds also hunt them."

TX.prompt: Read this sentence from the story: "Marcus wrote the date and location on the clipboard." The Latin root loc in location means —
TX.answer: place

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Figurative language & word relationships
concepts.summary: Interpret similes, metaphors, idioms and other figurative language and explain how word choice creates meaning. Grade focus: Explain similes, metaphors, idioms, adages and proverbs.
steps: Sort phrases into literal and figurative.
Draw what an idiom says vs what it means.
Identify similes and metaphors and say what is being compared.
Explain why the author used the figure of speech.
Use figurative language in writing.
concepts.check: Explain the meaning of a simile in a poem and why the poet used it.
concepts.misconception: Interpreting idioms literally.
concepts.supports: Idiom picture cards; bilingual idiom comparisons for ELLs.

NC.prompt: The poet calls the ocean "a restless giant." Explain this metaphor and what it shows about the ocean.
NC.answer: It compares the ocean to a huge, moving giant to show it is large, powerful and always moving.

MI.prompt: Jada says to look for tracks "that look like a tractor drove out of the ocean." This simile helps the reader understand that the tracks are —
MI.answer: wide and deep

TX.prompt: In the poem, the ocean "breathes in, then breathes out." What does this personification describe?
TX.answer: waves moving in and out

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Poetry, drama & point of view

steps: Read a poem, a script and a story about the same idea.

Identify the narrator and their pronouns.
Retell a scene from another character's point of view.
Explain how the form changes the reader's experience.
concepts.check: Explain how a story would change if told by a different character.
concepts.misconception: Confusing the author with the narrator.
concepts.supports: Readers' theater; point-of-view pronoun charts.

NC.prompt: Explain two differences between "The Ocean at Night" and "Turtle Patrol." Use the words stanza, line or rhyme.
NC.answer: The poem is written in lines and two stanzas with rhyme (out / about); the story is prose written in paragraphs with dialogue.

MI.prompt: Is "Turtle Patrol" told in first-person or third-person point of view? How do you know, and how would it change if Marcus told it?
MI.answer: Third person: the narrator uses he and Marcus. In first person we would hear Marcus's thoughts directly using I.

TX.prompt: How is the poem organized?
choices: in two stanzas of four lines each
TX.answer: in two stanzas of four lines each

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Compare & synthesize across texts
concepts.summary: Compare themes, topics and information across texts and integrate information from several sources. Grade focus: Compare treatment of similar themes and topics across cultures; integrate two texts on one topic.
steps: Read two texts on one topic and list facts from each.
Mark what is the same and what is different.
Explain what you learn from both together that neither gives alone.
Write a short synthesis paragraph citing both texts.
concepts.check: Use two articles to answer one question, citing both.
concepts.misconception: Summarizing each text separately with no comparison.
concepts.supports: Two-column notes; color code by source.

NC.prompt: Use information from both "Turtle Patrol" and the article to explain why volunteers mark sea turtle nests.
NC.answer: The article says volunteers mark nests so they are not disturbed; in the story Marcus puts stakes and tape around the nest so no one steps on it.

MI.prompt: How does the article help you understand why Marcus says, "We kept your spot safe"? Use one detail from each text.
MI.answer: The article explains hatchlings face many dangers and few survive; the story shows Marcus protecting the nest all summer.

TX.prompt: Which idea is found in BOTH the story and the article?
choices: Hatchlings head toward the water at night.
TX.answer: Hatchlings head toward the water at night.

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Opinion writing
concepts.summary: Write opinion pieces that state a point of view and support it with reasons and evidence. Grade focus: Support reasons with facts and details; group related ideas logically.

State an opinion and list reasons on a planner.
Find facts or examples that support each reason.
Draft with linking words (because, for example, therefore).
Revise for a strong conclusion.
concepts.check: Write an opinion paragraph with a clear claim, two reasons and evidence for each.
concepts.misconception: Listing reasons without evidence; switching opinions mid-piece.
concepts.supports: OREO planner (Opinion, Reason, Example, Opinion); sentence starters.

NC.prompt: Should beach towns require outdoor lights to be turned off during sea turtle nesting season? Write an opinion piece. State your opinion, support it with reasons and facts from "Turtle Patrol" and "Sea Turtle Hatchlings: A Risky Start," use linking words, and end with a conclusion.
NC.answer: Look for: clear opinion, logically ordered reasons supported by text facts, linking words and a concluding section.

MI.prompt: Your principal asks: Should beach towns require outdoor lights to be turned off during sea turtle nesting season? Write an opinion essay that uses information from both "Turtle Patrol" and "Sea Turtle Hatchlings: A Risky Start."
MI.answer: Scored on purpose and organization, evidence and elaboration, and conventions.

TX.prompt: Should beach towns require outdoor lights to be turned off during sea turtle nesting season? Write an argumentative essay that states your position and supports it with evidence from "Turtle Patrol" and "Sea Turtle Hatchlings: A Risky Start."
TX.answer: Scored on development and organization of ideas and on conventions.

NC.answer: Look for: introduction, grouped facts, precise vocabulary, linking words, concluding statement.

MI.prompt: Write an informational article for the school newsletter that explains why sea turtle hatchlings face danger and how people can help. Use details from "Sea Turtle Hatchlings: A Risky Start."
MI.answer: Scored on purpose and organization, evidence and elaboration, and conventions.

TX.prompt: Write an informational essay that explains why sea turtle hatchlings face danger and how people can help. Use evidence from "Sea Turtle Hatchlings: A Risky Start."
TX.answer: Scored on development and organization of ideas and on conventions.

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Narrative writing

Plan beginning, middle and end on a story map.
Draft a strong lead and add dialogue.
Revise to show feelings through actions and senses.
Edit and share.
concepts.check: Write a personal narrative scene that uses dialogue and a sensory detail.
concepts.misconception: Bed-to-bed stories that list every event at the same pace.
concepts.supports: Story maps; mentor sentences for leads and endings.

NC.prompt: Write a personal narrative about a time you helped protect or care for an animal or place. Use dialogue, description and transition words to show the order of events.
NC.answer: Look for: a clear situation, dialogue and description, a logical sequence and a conclusion.

MI.prompt: Retell the night the turtles hatched from the point of view of one hatchling.
MI.answer: Scored on narrative focus, development with dialogue and description, and conventions.

TX.prompt: Compose a personal narrative about a time you helped protect or care for an animal or place. (Narrative writing is taught in the TEKS but is not a STAAR essay type.)
TX.answer: Look for: focused structure, engaging details and edited conventions.

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Writing process & conventions

Draft quickly without stopping to fix spelling.
Revise with a single focus (add, remove, move, substitute).
Edit with a checklist for the conventions taught this unit.
Publish and reflect.

concepts.misconception: Treating revising and editing as the same thing.
concepts.supports: ARMS / CUPS checklists; peer conferencing protocols.

NC.prompt: Edit this sentence for capitalization, verb tense and punctuation: "marcus and jada walks the beach at sunrise last summer"
NC.answer: Marcus and Jada walked the beach at sunrise last summer.

MI.prompt: Which is the best way to fix this run-on sentence? "The hatchlings crawled toward the ocean they followed the moonlight."

The hatchlings crawled toward the ocean. They followed the moonlight.
The hatchlings crawled toward the ocean, they followed the moonlight.
the hatchlings crawled toward the ocean they followed the moonlight.
MI.answer: The hatchlings crawled toward the ocean. They followed the moonlight.

TX.prompt: A student wrote: "The hatchlings crawled toward the ocean they followed the moonlight." What is the best way to revise this sentence?
choices: The hatchlings crawled toward the ocean. They followed the moonlight.
Add a comma after the first word
TX.answer: The hatchlings crawled toward the ocean. They followed the moonlight.

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Short research projects
concepts.summary: Conduct short research projects, gather information from print and digital sources, take notes and list sources. Grade focus: Investigate different aspects of a topic; paraphrase in notes and list sources.

Locate two to three kid-friendly sources.
Take notes in your own words (paraphrase, not copy).
Sort notes into categories and draft.
Present findings and cite sources.
concepts.check: Paraphrase a paragraph from a source in your own words and record the source.
concepts.misconception: Copying sentences word for word.
concepts.supports: Note-taking templates; curated source sets.

NC.answer: Notes are paraphrased, sorted into categories, and both sources are listed.

MI.prompt: A student is researching: Why are bright lights dangerous to sea turtle hatchlings? Which source would be most useful?
choices: a story about a pirate ship
a wildlife agency web page about sea turtle nesting
MI.answer: a wildlife agency web page about sea turtle nesting

TX.prompt: A student is researching: Why are bright lights dangerous to sea turtle hatchlings? Which is a primary source?
choices: a volunteer's logbook of turtle nests found on Emerald Isle
a magazine summary of turtle research
TX.answer: a volunteer's logbook of turtle nests found on Emerald Isle

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Phonics, word analysis & fluency
concepts.summary: Decode multisyllabic words, read grade-level texts accurately and fluently with expression. Grade focus: Use letter-sound correspondences, syllabication and morphology to read unfamiliar multisyllabic words.

Practice decoding words in isolation, then in sentences.
Model fluent reading; echo and choral read.
Repeated reading with timed feedback.
Apply in independent connected text.
concepts.check: Read a grade-level passage aloud; check words correct per minute and expression.
concepts.misconception: Guessing from pictures or first letters instead of decoding.
concepts.supports: Small-group decoding intervention; decodable texts for older readers.

NC.prompt: Read these words from this grade's passages by breaking them into syllables: volunteers, hatchlings, instinct.
NC.answer: vol / un / teers; hatch / lings; in / stinct

MI.prompt: Read the first three paragraphs of "Turtle Patrol" aloud for one minute. The teacher records words correct per minute and rates expression.
MI.answer: Compare words correct per minute to grade 4 norms and note phrasing and expression.

TX.prompt: Divide each word into syllables, then read it: volunteers, hatchlings, instinct.
TX.answer: vol / un / teers; hatch / lings; in / stinct

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Cite text evidence & make inferences
concepts.summary: Ask and answer questions, refer to details and quote accurately to support what the text says and what can be inferred. Grade focus: Quote accurately when explaining and drawing inferences.
steps: Think-aloud: model noticing a clue and saying what it makes you think.
It Says / I Say / And So chart with partners.
Highlight the exact words that prove an answer.
Write answers with a frame: "I think ___ because the text says ___."
Independently answer inference questions with quoted evidence.
concepts.check: Answer an inference question about a short passage and quote the line that proves it.
concepts.misconception: Giving evidence from background knowledge rather than the text; quoting a line that is related but does not prove the point.
concepts.supports: Sentence frames, color-coded highlighting, partner talk before writing.

NC.prompt: What can you infer about why Priya "didn't answer right away"? Quote accurately from the text to support your inference.
NC.answer: She is thinking about the problem instead of giving up: "She was staring at the laptop screen" and "Now Priya wondered if he meant it."

MI.prompt: Part A: What does Andre's last line, "Information," show? Part B: Which sentence from earlier in the story does it connect to?
choices: He now agrees that mistakes can teach you.
He thinks the coach was wrong.
MI.answer: Part A: He now agrees that mistakes can teach you. Part B: "Mr. Haynes, their coach, had told them that every crash was information."

TX.prompt: Which sentence best shows that Priya uses evidence to solve the problem?
choices: "Every time it spins, it's after the second turn," she said slowly.
TX.answer: "Every time it spins, it's after the second turn," she said slowly.

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Theme, central message & summary
concepts.summary: Determine the theme or central message of a story, poem or drama and summarize the text. Grade focus: Determine a theme, including how characters respond to challenges, and summarize.
steps: Separate topic (friendship) from theme (true friends tell the truth).
Track what the main character learns or how they change.
Turn the lesson into a statement that applies to anyone.
Summarize with Somebody-Wanted-But-So-Then.
Compare themes across two texts.
concepts.check: State the theme of a fable in a full sentence and give two details that support it.
concepts.misconception: Naming a one-word topic as the theme; retelling every event instead of summarizing.
concepts.supports: Theme word bank, topic-to-theme sorting cards, short fables first.

NC.prompt: Determine a theme of "Twelve Seconds," including how the characters respond to the challenge. Then summarize the story.
NC.answer: Theme: Failures give you information that helps you improve. The robot keeps crashing; instead of quitting, Priya studies the pattern, they find the sensor problem, fix it and finish in eleven seconds.

MI.prompt: Part A: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story? Part B: Which two details best support it?
choices: Studying your mistakes can lead to success.
MI.answer: Part A: Studying your mistakes can lead to success. Part B: Priya notices the robot always spins after the second turn; the fixed robot finishes in eleven seconds.

TX.prompt: What theme does the author develop through Priya and Andre's actions? Use evidence from the story to support your answer.
TX.answer: Scored on a stated theme with evidence, for example: don't give up after failure; Priya studies the code and they test the sensor until Bolt succeeds.

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Characters, setting & plot
concepts.summary: Describe characters, their motivations and changes, and how setting and events shape the story. Grade focus: Compare and contrast two or more characters, settings or events.
steps: Act out a scene and name what the character feels.
Separate outside traits from inside traits with evidence.
Map the plot: problem, events, climax, resolution.
Explain how the setting influences the problem.
Compare two characters with a Venn diagram and evidence.
concepts.check: How does the main character change from beginning to end? Use two pieces of evidence.
concepts.misconception: Listing physical traits only; confusing feelings with traits.
concepts.supports: Character trait word bank; plot mountain organizer.

NC.prompt: Compare and contrast how Priya and Andre respond to the robot's crash. Use specific details.
NC.answer: Andre wants to drop out and slumps in his chair; Priya stays calm, studies the code and finds a pattern. Both work together on the fix.

MI.prompt: Which word best describes Priya? Quote a sentence that shows it.
MI.answer: observant; "Every time it spins, it's after the second turn."

TX.prompt: What conflict do the characters face?
choices: They argue about who will drive the robot.
Their robot cannot finish the course, and the competition is in four days.
TX.answer: Their robot cannot finish the course, and the competition is in four days.

concepts.subject: ela
concepts.name: Main idea & key details
concepts.summary: Determine the main or central idea of an informational text and explain how key details support it. Grade focus: Determine two or more main ideas and explain how details support them.
steps: Sort details under a given main idea (table and legs).
Ask "What is this mostly about?" for each paragraph.
Combine paragraph gists into a main idea statement.
Explain how each key detail supports the main idea.
Summarize without opinions.
concepts.check: Write the main idea of an article in one sentence and list three supporting details.
concepts.misconception: Picking an interesting detail as the main idea; stating only the topic.
concepts.supports: Main-idea table graphic organizer; shorter texts with headings.

NC.prompt: Determine two main ideas of "Failing Forward" and explain how key details support each.
NC.answer: 1) Engineers follow a design cycle that expects failure (define, prototype, test, improve). 2) Failure gives useful data (the Wright brothers tested about 200 wing shapes).

MI.prompt: Part A: What is the central idea of the article? Part B: Which detail best supports it?
choices: Engineers use failure as information to improve their designs.
MI.answer: Part A: Engineers use failure as information to improve their designs. Part B: The Wright brothers' wind tunnel tests helped them design the 1903 Flyer.

TX.prompt: Which detail best supports the idea that failure gives engineers useful data?
choices: People picture inventors with brilliant ideas.
The Wright brothers tested about 200 wing shapes in a wind tunnel.
The cycle may repeat dozens of times.
A prototype is a simple early model.
TX.answer: The Wright brothers tested about 200 wing shapes in a wind tunnel.

concepts.name: Text structure & features
concepts.summary: Use text features and describe overall structure (chronology, comparison, cause/effect, problem/solution). Grade focus: Compare the overall structure in two or more texts.
steps: Text-feature scavenger hunt in a nonfiction book.
Introduce signal words for each structure.
Match paragraphs to structure graphic organizers.
Explain why the author chose that structure.
Compare structures across two texts on one topic.
concepts.check: Identify the structure of a paragraph and name the signal words that show it.
concepts.misconception: Choosing a structure from one signal word; ignoring the purpose.
concepts.supports: Signal-word anchor chart; structure graphic organizers.

NC.prompt: Compare the overall structure of paragraph 2 of the article with the structure of the story.

MI.prompt: Select all the signal words in paragraph 2 that show sequence.
MI.answer: First; Next; Then; Finally

TX.prompt: Why does the author begin the article by describing how people often picture inventors?
choices: To list the steps of the design cycle
To give the meaning of prototype
To introduce an idea the article will correct

NC.prompt: In paragraph 2 of "Failing Forward," what does prototype mean? Explain how the author helps you understand it.

MI.prompt: Part A: What does wildly mean in "The readings jumped wildly"? Part B: Which phrase helps you understand it?
MI.answer: Part A: in a sudden, uncontrolled way. Part B: "whenever the room got brighter" (the readings changed a lot).

TX.prompt: The prefix proto- in prototype means —
TX.answer: first

MI.prompt: The shoebox is "taped around the sensor like a tiny tunnel." What does this simile help the reader understand?

MI.prompt: "Twelve Seconds" is told in third person but follows Priya's thoughts. How does this point of view affect how the reader understands the turning point?

TX.prompt: Which line from the poem shows a rhyme with "sailed"?

a map, a ladder, a key,
to the builder I will be.

story.title: The Seed Swap
story.text:
Every spring, Grandma Rose hosted a seed swap on her front porch. Neighbors brought envelopes of seeds and traded them like baseball cards.

This year, Lila wanted to bring something special. She had saved seeds from her sunflower, the tallest one on Maple Street. But when she opened her jar, the seeds were gray and fuzzy with mold.

"They're ruined," Lila said. Her chin wobbled.

Grandma Rose looked at the jar. "Seeds need to stay dry," she said gently. "Next fall, we'll dry them on a screen first."

Lila sat on the steps while neighbors traded. She had nothing to give. Then Mr. Okafor waved her over. "I have too many pepper seeds," he said. "Would you help me count them into envelopes?"

Lila counted carefully, ten seeds in each envelope. By the end of the afternoon, she had filled twenty envelopes. Mr. Okafor handed her one. "For your hard work," he said.

That night, Lila wrote a label for a new jar: DRY FIRST.

article.title: How Seeds Travel
article.text:
Plants cannot walk, but their seeds still find new places to grow. Seeds travel in several ways.

Some seeds ride the wind. A dandelion seed has a fluffy top that works like a parachute. A gust of wind can carry it far across a field.

Other seeds hitch a ride on animals. Burdock seeds are covered in tiny hooks. When a dog brushes past, the hooks catch its fur. Later, the seeds fall off in a new spot.

Some seeds float. A coconut has a hard, waterproof shell, so it can drift across the ocean and land on a faraway beach.

Animals also move seeds by eating fruit. A bird eats a berry, flies away, and drops the seed somewhere new.

Because seeds spread out, young plants do not have to compete with their parent plant for sunlight and water.

poem.title: Sunflower
poem.text:
I am a ladder of green
climbing up to the sky,
my face a bright yellow clock
that follows the sun going by.

In the morning I look east,
at night I bow my head;
the bees hum their thank-you songs
as I tuck my seeds to bed.

story.title: Turtle Patrol
story.text:
At sunrise, Marcus and his older cousin Jada walked the beach at Emerald Isle with a clipboard and a flashlight. They were volunteers on the Turtle Patrol.

"Look for tracks that look like a tractor drove out of the ocean," Jada said.

Marcus yawned. He had wanted to sleep in. Walking in cold sand at six in the morning did not feel like summer vacation.

Then he saw them: two wide lines of flipper marks leading from the waves to the dunes. At the end, the sand was piled in a messy circle.

"A nest!" Marcus shouted, forgetting to be tired.

Jada showed him how to place wooden stakes and orange tape around the nest so no one would step on it. Marcus wrote the date and location on the clipboard, pressing hard so his letters were neat.

For the rest of the summer, Marcus woke up before his alarm. He checked the nest every morning. Sixty days later, he watched tiny turtles, each one smaller than his palm, scramble toward the moonlit water.

"Go on," he whispered. "We kept your spot safe."

article.title: Sea Turtle Hatchlings: A Risky Start
article.text:
Loggerhead sea turtles nest on North Carolina beaches every summer. A female crawls onto the sand at night, digs a hole, and lays about 100 eggs. Then she returns to the sea and never sees her babies.

After about two months, the hatchlings break out of their shells. They usually leave the nest at night, when the sand is cool and fewer predators are awake. The hatchlings find the ocean by crawling toward the brightest horizon, which is normally the moonlight on the water.

Today, that instinct can cause problems. Lights from houses and streets can confuse hatchlings, so they crawl the wrong way. Ghost crabs and birds also hunt them.

People can help. Many beach towns ask residents to turn off outdoor lights during nesting season. Volunteers mark nests so they are not disturbed. Scientists estimate that only about 1 in 1,000 hatchlings survives to adulthood, so every protected nest matters.

poem.title: The Ocean at Night
poem.text:
The ocean is a restless giant
who breathes in, then breathes out,
his silver blanket of moonlight
rumpled and tossed about.

He hums a low and salty song
to the dunes along the shore,
and little turtles answer him
by racing to his door.

story.title: Twelve Seconds
story.text:
The robot rolled three feet, beeped, and spun in a slow circle until it crashed into the table leg.

"Again?" groaned Priya. The regional robotics competition was in four days, and their robot, Bolt, still could not finish the twelve-second course.

Andre slumped in his chair. "Maybe we should just drop out. The other teams have been building since August."

Priya didn't answer right away. She was staring at the laptop screen, where line after line of code glowed. Mr. Haynes, their coach, had told them that every crash was information. At the time, it had sounded like something adults say to make you feel better. Now Priya wondered if he meant it.

"Every time it spins, it's after the second turn," she said slowly. "What if the turn isn't the problem? What if it's the sensor reading the black tape?"

Andre sat up. They tested the sensor with a flashlight, then with the lights off. The readings jumped wildly whenever the room got brighter.

It took two more afternoons and one shoebox, taped around the sensor like a tiny tunnel, but on Friday, Bolt crossed the finish line in eleven seconds.

Andre grinned. "Information," he said.

article.title: Failing Forward: How Engineers Learn from Mistakes
article.text:
When people picture inventors, they often imagine a brilliant idea that works on the first try. In reality, engineers expect their designs to fail, and they plan for it.

Engineers follow a process often called the engineering design cycle. First, they define the problem and research what has already been tried. Next, they brainstorm ideas and build a prototype, a simple early model. Then they test the prototype, collect data, and look for weaknesses. Finally, they improve the design and test again. The cycle may repeat dozens of times.

Failure gives engineers useful data. When the Wright brothers' early gliders did not lift as much as they expected, the brothers built a small wind tunnel in 1901 and tested about 200 wing shapes. Those measurements helped them design the 1903 Wright Flyer, which made the first powered, controlled airplane flight.

Many engineering teams today test parts until they break on purpose. By finding the weakest point in a safe test, they can make the final product stronger. As one saying puts it, it is better to fail early, fail small, and learn fast.

poem.title: Prototype
poem.text:
My first try was a paper boat
that sank before it sailed;
my second was a cardboard kite
that dove, and twirled, and failed.

But every crumpled, soggy wreck
was whispering a clue,
a stepping stone of "not quite yet"
that led me to "it's true!"

So call my failures what they are:
a map, a ladder, a key,
each one a door I opened up
to the builder I will be.

story.title: Below the Surface
story.text:
Rosa had imagined the research ship would feel like a floating laboratory. Instead, on her first morning aboard the Seeker, it felt like a washing machine. The deck rolled under her feet, and her stomach rolled with it.

"You'll get your sea legs," said Dr. Hale, the chief scientist, handing her a cracker. "Everyone does. Eventually."

Rosa was the youngest person on the expedition, invited because her science fair project on ocean sound had won a state award. Now, staring at the gray water, she wondered whether the judges had made a mistake.

On the third day, the crew lowered the remotely operated vehicle, a yellow robot the size of a small car, into the water. Rosa sat in the control room beside the pilot, watching the screens. At 200 meters, the blue light faded to dusk. At 1,000 meters, the screens went black except for the glow of the robot's lamps.

Then something flickered at the edge of the light: a ribbon of blue sparks drifting past like a slow firework.

"Bioluminescence," whispered the pilot. "Something down there makes its own light."

Rosa forgot about her stomach. For two hours she logged every flash, noting the depth and the time. When the robot surfaced, Dr. Hale read her notes and raised an eyebrow.

"These are careful observations," she said. "Most people just stare."

That night, Rosa stood at the rail. The ship still rolled, but she rocked with it now, the way the ocean seemed to ask her to. Somewhere beneath her, in the dark, the sparks were still drifting. She had a feeling she would spend her life trying to understand them.

article.title: Mapping the Deep
article.text:
More than 70 percent of Earth's surface is covered by ocean, yet scientists have more detailed maps of the surface of Mars than of much of the seafloor. Why is the bottom of our own planet so hard to see?

The answer is water. Light fades quickly as it travels down through the ocean, and below about 1,000 meters no sunlight reaches at all. The cameras and satellites that map land cannot see through that much water.

Instead, scientists map the seafloor with sound. A ship sends pulses of sound toward the bottom and measures how long the echoes take to return. Because sound travels through seawater at a known speed, about 1,500 meters per second, the time tells how deep the water is. Modern ships use multibeam sonar, which sends out a fan of sound beams to map a wide strip of seafloor at once.

The work is slow. A ship can map only the strip beneath its path, and the ocean is enormous. An international project called Seabed 2030 is working to map the entire ocean floor in detail by the year 2030. When the project began in 2017, only about 6 percent of the seafloor had been mapped in high detail. By 2024, the total had reached about a quarter.

Better maps matter. They help ships navigate safely, show where undersea cables can be laid, and reveal underwater mountains and canyons where sea life gathers. They also help scientists predict how tsunamis will travel. Every new strip of map is a step toward knowing our planet's last unexplored frontier.

poem.title: The Deep
poem.text:
I am the deep, the patient dark,
the room no sun has entered.
I keep my secrets folded small
in canyons, cold and centered.

You send your songs of sound to me;
I hum them back, unhurried.
You count the seconds of my voice
and draw me, slow, unworried.

But some things I will not explain:
the sparks that drift like embers,
the lanterns carried by the fish,
the dark that still remembers.

story.title: Puddle Day
story.text:
Rain fell all morning. Nia pressed her nose to the window.

"When can I go out?" she asked.

"When the rain stops," said Papa.

At last the sun came out. Nia put on her red boots. She found a big puddle. Splash! Splash! The water jumped up high.

Then Nia saw a worm in the puddle. She gently picked it up and set it in the grass. "Now you are safe," she said.

article.title: Where Does Rain Go?
article.text:
Rain falls from clouds.

Some rain soaks into the ground. Plants drink it with their roots.

Some rain runs into streams and ponds.

When the sun shines, puddles dry up. The water goes back up into the air. Later it falls again as rain.

poem.title: Rain Song
poem.text:
Pitter, patter on the roof,
Drip, drop by the door,
Rain is tapping out a song,
Then it pours and pours!

Puddles shine like mirrors,
Clouds roll far away,
Sun peeks out and smiles at me,
Now it's time to play.

story.title: Max and the Bee
story.text:
Max was eating a peach on the porch. A bee landed on the table. Max jumped up. "Go away!" he yelled, and he waved his arms.

"Stay still," said his sister, June. "Bees sting when they are scared."

Max held very still. The bee walked across the table. It sipped a drop of peach juice. Then it flew to the flowers by the fence.

"It just wanted a snack," said June.

Max smiled. "I guess we both like sweet things," he said.

article.title: Busy Bees
article.text:
Home Sweet Hive
Honeybees live together in a hive. One queen bee lays the eggs. Worker bees do the other jobs.

Flower Helpers
Worker bees fly from flower to flower to drink sweet nectar. As they fly, yellow pollen sticks to their legs. The pollen helps flowers make seeds.

Bee Dance
Back at the hive, bees turn nectar into honey. A bee can do a special dance to tell other bees where to find flowers.

poem.title: Buzz
poem.text:
Buzz, buzz, in the sun,
Busy bee has work to be done.
Flower to flower, all day long,
Humming a happy honey song.

story.title: The Picnic Parade
story.text:
Carlos and his grandpa spread a blanket under the oak tree. They had sandwiches, grapes and a big slice of watermelon.

After lunch, Carlos dropped a piece of watermelon in the grass. Soon a line of tiny black ants marched toward it.

"Grandpa, they're stealing our food!" Carlos said.

Grandpa knelt down. "Look closer," he said. "They are working together. One ant found the food. Now the others are following her trail."

Carlos watched for a long time. The ants carried tiny bits of watermelon back to a hole near the tree. Not one ant gave up.

On the way home, Carlos had an idea. "Tomorrow, let's bring a piece of watermelon just for them," he said.

Grandpa laughed. "Now you are a real ant scientist."

article.title: Ants Work Together
article.text:
A Big Family
Ants live in large groups called colonies. A colony can have thousands of ants. The queen lays eggs. Worker ants take care of the young, build tunnels and find food.

Following the Trail
When a worker ant finds food, it leaves a trail of scent on the way back to the nest. Other ants smell the trail with their antennae and follow it to the food.

Strong and Small
Ants are tiny, but they are strong. Many ants can lift things heavier than their own bodies. By working together, ants can move food much bigger than one ant.

poem.title: Ant Line
poem.text:
One by one and two by two,
Marching where the grasses grew,
Tiny feet that never stop,
Carry crumbs up to the top.

Over pebbles, under leaves,
Past the roots of shady trees,
Little helpers, side by side,
Working hard with ant-sized pride.
